name: David Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm David, 27, lead travel-claims clerk at a small insurer. I have a bachelor's degree and am good at matching an airport report, a receipt and a policy limit, though the lead pay is low and local insurers are few. I use AI every day to sort anonymous receipt examples, then check real files myself. My partner works variable café shifts, and we rent with no children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell travellers the lost-bag receipt and the policy limit both matter. I lead a small travel-claims paperwork team at an insurer, and I use AI every day to sort anonymised receipt types before checking an actual file against the airport report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a small helper, the job probably lasts, but our finances are tight. I'm 27 with a bachelor's degree and strong claim skills, yet the insurer pays below the usual lead rate; my partner has variable café shifts, we rent, and two weeks of expenses are saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep matching delayed-bag receipts to airport reports and the policy limit. We'd stop the 24 monthly gaming service and put that money in a rent account whenever both incomes arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next rent payment, even if the technology is boring. A missed café shift would use up our spare money fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which dates made the coat receipt odd?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A traveller claimed a new coat while waiting for a suitcase, but the receipt was dated before the flight. The airport report showed the bag really was delayed. I asked the delayed-bag traveller for the right coat receipt instead of denying the whole claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How reliable are café shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I have no children. We split bills, but I do not count a perfect café rota as guaranteed income.

I'd ask for **correct purchase dates** before denying a delayed-bag claim.
think: I have **two weeks saved** and variable café income beside my low lead pay.
I see **few local insurance roles** if my team shrinks.
do: Keep **matching bag receipts** to airport reports and policy limits.
Cancel **gaming service** from the next bill.
Save its **24 monthly fee** whenever both incomes arrive.
feel: **Anxious** about rent and uncertain café shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could read receipts and draft claim replies before a clerk sees the airport report. I want it to flag a date mismatch without calling every traveller a liar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team could shrink because checking and answering are the work. I learn tools quickly, but two weeks saved means I cannot shrug off even a modest cut in paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the claims manager to approve a three-week AI receipt trial on old anonymous bag files, including the coat dated before the flight and a valid meal receipt. If both are handled correctly without a false denial, I'd use it for one queue of drafts with a named clerk reviewing every refusal; we'd postpone a planned music festival until paid hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours, but the trial is worth doing if the traveller can correct it. A date flag should start a question, not end a claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which receipt should pass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The meal receipt was during the delay and under the policy limit, so it should pass. The coat needs another date, not a fraud label automatically attached to the traveller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the festival wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The festival tickets are not bought yet. My partner and I can keep the money while the insurer decides how many people it will pay.

I'd require **clerk review** before any AI-drafted refusal.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** as receipt checks automate.
I cannot cover **rent after a cut** on two weeks saved.
do: Trial **AI receipt sorting** three weeks only with manager approval and both bag-file cases.
Use it for **one draft queue** only if both pass and a named clerk checks each refusal.
Delay **music festival** until paid staffing hours are clear.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, interested in a correctable date flag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could handle claim paperwork before baggage robots arrive around 2031. A traveller still needs a person to correct a wrong refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the insurer could cut my lead post quickly when cheaper AI reads and answers receipts. My partner's café pay alone cannot cover rent and food, and two weeks saved would run out before a long local search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the airport service desk and two nearby insurers about actual paid travel-support or claims jobs, wages and start dates. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose pay with my partner's lowest recent café hours covers rent, food and travel, checking whether its start date leaves a gap; if none qualifies or a gap remains, I'd seek available paid shifts and contact the landlord before rent is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about what would happen to my pay, though I can check real openings now. Being quick with an AI tool will not make another insurer post a job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a hiring manager the anonymised coat and meal receipts and explain why only one needed a date question. I would remove the traveller's name and policy number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would café hours affect an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would use the lowest café month in our calculation. If a new job's hours make those shifts impossible, my signed wage alone has to cover the bills.

say: I'd keep **traveller corrections** if 2028 thinking AI replaces paperwork.
I'd check **real paid openings** before promising a fallback.
think: I expect **my lead post** could disappear quickly.
I cannot cover **rent and food** on café shifts and two weeks saved.
do: Ask **airport desk** and two insurers about paid support and claims openings, wages and start dates.

Seek **paid shifts** if no role qualifies or a gap remains; contact landlord before arrears.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible lead-post cut with only two weeks saved.
S2.quote: Being quick with an AI tool will not make another insurer post a job for me.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches desk claims before 2031 baggage robots.
His wage floor uses **low café income**, falling to his signed wage alone if shifts cannot continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives us time to look at the airport city where more insurers operate. Thinking AI reaches claims paperwork first, and baggage robots follow around 2034; a move does not make my desk work safe by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider moving for a genuine claims job, not just a bigger list of vacancies. My partner would leave café shifts here, and our two-week reserve cannot pay a new deposit and van from hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask airport-city insurers for posted paid claims roles, signed wages, start dates and relocation help, then talk through any real offer with my partner. If my salary alone covers new rent, food and travel until my partner finds work, the employer pays the deposit and first moving bill, the job starts in time for the lease and first rent, and my partner agrees, we'd move after 2031 only on a signed offer; otherwise I'd keep paid claims work here while offered and seek local paid work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the main wage and the move, but five years lets me price it properly. A crowded job board is not a pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which dates would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the job start with the lease start and the first month's rent. If the firm cannot cover the deposit or first moving bill, we stay in this town and apply locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would your partner leave café work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would need to decide before giving notice at the café. We will not count café pay after moving, or assume my partner can pick up shifts in a new city immediately.

I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches claims before 2034 baggage robots.

feel: **Anxious** about pay and relocation costs, able to check real terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives me more time to build a real rent buffer, but thinking AI still reaches claims before baggage robots around 2039. I would keep the correction route open for a wrong date flag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37, with no reason to pretend retirement is close. Today we still have two weeks saved and variable café shifts, so the long card does not itself make rent secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the coat-and-meal case in our checklist and save the cancelled 24 gaming fee whenever both incomes arrive, then review the rent buffer every six months. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid claims work only while real hours exist; if they end, I'd seek a signed job covering rent, food and travel, without assuming a city move or my partner's future shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's rent, though a decade offers room to try a paid move if one appears. I would rather see the moving deposit in an employer's written offer than in my imagination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the checklist ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checklist should ask for the flight date, airport report and receipt date before anyone calls a claim false. Another clerk should be able to ask the same question without making a traveller feel accused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move without your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will decide any move together. We have no children to plan for, but we still need both names on a lease before promising a new city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead claims wage could go before another paid role opens. Written cut timing, real jobs with start dates and a landlord conversation before arrears would help us keep rent current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a date flag means a traveller lied. A receipt question is a conversation, not a fraud verdict; I want the claimant to have room to correct the file.

headlineQuote: A receipt question is a conversation, not a fraud verdict; I want the claimant to have room to correct the file.
portrait: David, **27**, leads travel-claims paperwork after a bachelor's degree and checks receipts against airport reports and policy limits.
His **low lead pay**, variable café household income, two-week reserve and few local insurer jobs make rent precarious.
He uses AI **daily** for anonymous examples and tests receipt sorting with manager approval and clerk review before live drafts.
Fast 2028 AGI makes him **anxious**; signed replacement pay must cover bills even if café shifts end.
A possible city move needs **partner agreement**, a real paid job, employer-covered relocation and his solo wage covering new rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his lead claims wage before another paid local role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut timing**, real job start dates and landlord contact before arrears would help.
